paras: The Red Shirt seizure of the Darlington polls was the occupation of Darlington, South Carolina, by armed Red-Shirt Democrats on the night of November 1, 1880, and their control of the court-house polls on election day, November 2. According to a Darlington dispatch, Republicans who tried to vote had revolvers pointed at their heads, and a thousand or more were kept from voting. Northern Republican papers reported it as one of the frauds by which South Carolina was carried for Hancock.

The episode came amid statewide Republican complaints about the 1880 election, including claims that Democrats planted cannon in Charleston wards and threw out Republican ballots. Chief Supervisor S. T. Poinier's returns, as reported from Charleston, named Darlington among counties where precincts expected to give Republican majorities were never opened.

The Darlington correspondent wrote that the "Red-shirt Democracy" took possession of the town about sunset on Monday and camped all night around the public square. Through the night they cheered for Hancock and fired guns, pistols and old anvils used as cannon. Arms and ammunition had been stored in several stores, and the men who held the polls were, in the correspondent's words, "gangs of roughs" brought from Kellytown, Hartsville and Lydia in the same county.

On election morning the ballot-box was placed in the court house, where no Republican supervisor or officer was allowed near the poll. Red-Shirts held the entrances in large numbers and let no one pass who was not known to be a Democrat. Several Republicans who demanded admission had revolvers pointed at their heads and were told to go home. After waiting three or four hours the Republicans left, and the dispatch put those deprived of their votes at a thousand "and perhaps more". The Darlington accounts name no individual voter and do not state the race of either side.

The Attorney-General directed Federal officials in South Carolina to arrest persons guilty of complicity in election frauds, an order that covered the whole state. No report of arrests or prosecutions for the Darlington events appears in the coverage. In December, Samuel Lee, the Republican candidate in the First Congressional District, served notice contesting John S. Richardson's seat. Lee alleged violence, intimidation and the rejection of many qualified voters at the Darlington Court-House poll and asked that its vote be thrown out; he also charged that "colored voters" were denied the ballot at every precinct in the district.

The story first appeared in a Chicago Tribune Washington special of November 6, which folded the Darlington dispatch into a list of "frauds of the most astounding character" in South Carolina. On November 8 the Wheeling Intelligencer printed the Darlington letter in full under the headline "The Red Shirt in Politics. How South Carolina's Vote was Secured for Hancock and English." Western papers carried only a one-sentence wire version: the Sacramento Record-Union and the Gold Hill News, the latter under "Carolina Bulldosing," on November 8, and the Canton Advocate in Dakota Territory in condensed form on November 18.

Every account came from Republican-leaning papers or Republican sources, and all framed the events as partisan fraud against "Republicans" rather than in racial terms. No Democratic or South Carolina newspaper account of the Darlington events appears in the coverage.

reader.title: Red Shirt seizure of the Darlington polls (1880)
bases: Armed Red-Shirts occupied the town and the court-house polls, threatened would-be Republican voters with revolvers and kept them from voting; no one is reported killed or hurt at Darlington (A1, A4).

The Darlington dispatch (A4, summarized in A1) is the only detailed account, but Samuel Lee's separate contest notice independently alleges violence, intimidation and rejection of qualified voters at the Darlington Court-House poll (A9); all sources are Republican-side and no Democratic or local account was found.

accounts.label: Darlington correspondent (Nov. 5 dispatch)
accounts.gist: Red-Shirts camped armed on the square Monday night, took over the court-house polls, kept out every Republican, put revolvers to the heads of some who demanded to vote, and deprived a thousand or more of their votes; the 'gangs of roughs' came from Kellytown, Hartsville and Lydia.

accounts.label: Chicago Tribune Washington special
accounts.gist: Repeats the Darlington dispatch in summary alongside statewide reports of fraud, cannon in Charleston and the Attorney-General's arrest order.

accounts.label: Chief Supervisor's returns (Charleston dispatch)
accounts.gist: Lists Darlington among counties where precincts expected to return Republican majorities were never opened and 'various outrages' occurred.

accounts.label: Contestant Samuel Lee
accounts.gist: Alleges repeating, ballot-stuffing, violence, intimidation and the rejection of many qualified voters at Darlington Court-House and other Darlington precincts.

framing.detail: The Wheeling Intelligencer headed the dispatch 'The Red Shirt in Politics. How South Carolina's Vote was Secured for Hancock and English' and spoke of 'gangs of roughs'.
The Chicago Tribune set Darlington among 'frauds of the most astounding character' in South Carolina.
Western papers carried one-sentence or condensed wire versions, the Gold Hill News under 'Carolina Bulldosing'.
The National Republican headed the Charleston returns 'A State That Was Carried by Barefaced Fraud'.

record_check.dossier: Began Monday night Nov. 1 at sunset; the seizure of the polls and threats to voters were on election day, Nov. 2, 1880.
Armed gathering plus seizure of the polls, blocking of voters, and threats with revolvers pointed at voters' heads.
Unnamed Republican voters, a thousand or more, and Republican election officers; race not stated in the Darlington accounts.
Red-Shirt Democrats, including men brought from Kellytown, Hartsville and Lydia.
Targets were Republican voters and election officers; several were threatened at gunpoint and about a thousand kept from voting.
First report 1880-11-07 (Chicago Tribune); at least four papers carried the Darlington story, plus later district-wide reports.
